papers.title: Chromosome-scale comparative genomics reveals a genomic mosaic across the documented Hattan sake-brewing rice lineage
papers.abstract: Background: Breeding pedigrees record crosses and selections but do not reveal how the documented relationships are reflected in descendant genomes. Therefore, whole-genome summaries can mask local inheritance patterns generated by recombination and segregation. To examine how documented relationships are reflected across genomic scales, we generated chromosome-scale assemblies of the Hattanso landrace and four cultivars from the documented Hattan sake-brewing rice lineage of Hiroshima, Japan. We then analyzed genome-wide and local relationships using small variants, structural variants, and gene presence-absence variation. Results: The five assemblies ranged from 375.78 to 378.94 Mb in length, with scaffold N50 values of 30.25-30.43 Mb and 99.8% BUSCO completeness. Single-nucleotide variant data identified Hattan Nos. 10 and 35 as the closest pair at the genome-wide scale, a relationship also supported by protein sequence alignment. This relationship was recovered on 9 of the 12 chromosomes, but genomic relationships varied among local regions. Classification of 500-kb windows based on predefined allele-sharing patterns associated with documented breeding steps assigned 51.91% of the nuclear genome to lineage-pattern categories and identified 143 candidate transition intervals. Publicly available reads from Shuho broadly supported the Hattan No. 35 state, consistent with the recorded Hattan No. 10 x Shuho parentage of Hattan No. 35. Hattan-nishiki Nos. 1 and 2, selected from the recorded Hattan No. 35 x Akitsuho cross, exhibited distinct genomic configurations, with differences across all three variant classes concentrated on Chr12. A 1-Mb region on Chr4 contained single-nucleotide variants, small indels, and structural variants predominantly shared by Hattanso and the four derived cultivars. Functional enrichment analysis of lineage-associated gene sets identified pectinesterase-related functions in the Hattan No. 10-specific set and a diterpenoid-related signal in the Hattan-nishiki No. 2-specific set. Conclusions: The documented Hattan sake-brewing rice lineage exhibits a spatially heterogeneous genomic mosaic, in which a strong genome-wide relationship coexists with local variation in lineage-associated states. Integrating nucleotide-scale, structural, and gene-content variation across genomic scales thus complements pedigree records and helps prioritize candidate regions and genes for future functional and breeding studies.

papers.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of the hydrozoan jellyfish Cladonema pacificum
papers.abstract: The hydrozoan jellyfish Cladonema pacificum, which possesses experimentally tractable polyp and medusa stages, is an emerging cnidarian model for studies of regeneration, development, physiology, and behavior. Although experimental techniques have been established for this species, the lack of a chromosome-level reference genome has limited genome-wide and comparative analyses. Here, we present the first chromosome-level genome assembly of C. pacificum generated using HiFi long-read sequencing and Hi-C technology. The representative haploid assembly comprises 15 chromosome-scale scaffolds and 121 additional scaffolds, spanning 504.0 Mb with a scaffold N50 of 32.1 Mb. Gene annotation integrating RNA-seq, PacBio Iso-Seq, and protein homology identified 17,206 protein-coding genes, of which 95.7% received at least one functional annotation. Phylogenomic and macrosynteny analyses further confirmed the placement of C. pacificum within Hydrozoa and revealed extensive chromosome-scale conservation with other hydrozoan genomes. This genomic resource provides a valuable foundation for comparative genomics and future molecular, cellular, and evolutionary studies using C. pacificum as an emerging hydrozoan model.

papers.title: Reference genomes for Australian Cryptosporidium hominis and C. parvum from humans
papers.abstract: Cryptosporidium hominis and C. parvum are important protozoan pathogens of humans worldwide, and genomic surveillance is increasingly being used to investigate transmission and outbreaks. However, no complete Cryptosporidium genome is available from Australia, and many common Cryptosporidium gp60 subtypes lack high-quality genome assemblies worldwide. This study generated the first Australian reference genomes for two clinically relevant, zoonotic Cryptosporidium species, C. hominis and C. parvum from human hosts, as well as a scaffold-level genome for Australian C. meleagridis. Oocysts were purified from eleven clinical faecal samples and whole-genome sequencing was performed using short-read technologies. Three samples belonging to different species were also sequenced using long-read technology, with assemblies generated, telomere recovery undertaken and genomes annotated. High-quality reference C. hominis IaA12R3 genome (8 T2T chromosomes, 9.2 Mb, 4069 genes, 98.4% completeness), near-complete C. parvum IIaA20G3R1 genome (8 chromosomes, 9.2 Mb, 4004 genes, 98.2% completeness), and a draft C. meleagridis IIIgA31 genome (113 scaffolds, 9.3 Mb, 4075 genes, 97.2% completeness) were generated and had high nucleotide similarity (98-99%), gene cluster orthology (99%) and genome synteny relative to available international reference genomes. Phylogenomic analyses with global C. hominis and C. parvum genomes were performed to characterise the relationships of Australian isolates globally showing Australian C. hominis and C. parvum forming well-supported clades with North American European isolates. Whole-genome analyses of eight Australian C. hominis isolates revealed markedly better resolution of genetic relationships than gp60 subtyping alone. This study provides the resources for national genomic surveillance in Australia and expands the genomic representation of clinically relevant Cryptosporidium subtypes. Broader application of genomic surveillance has the potential to enhance outbreak investigation, improve understanding of transmission dynamics and support One Health approaches to cryptosporidiosis control.

papers.title: Structural Complexity in the Maize Pangenome Graph Is Generated by Transposable Elements and Sorted by Selection
papers.abstract: Pangenome graphs capture the structural variation that linear references miss, but what generates their complex regions, whether these are targets of selection and whether the structural context of a gene affects its expression is unknown. These questions were addressed with a graph of 58 chromosome level maize assemblies (57 inbred lines and a teosinte accession), a genome dominated by transposable elements (TEs). Between the segments shared by all assemblies, the conserved intervals, bubbles open where assemblies diverge; every bubble's complexity was scored by the number and length of its paths and bubbles were classified as high, medium or low complexity. TEs are 96% of the annotations in high complexity bubbles, whereas genes concentrate in low complexity bubbles and conserved intervals; genes confined to complex bubbles are enriched for transposase activity, chromatin constituents and defence responses. To test for selection, Tajima's D was computed in 10 kb windows from 38.5 million SNPs of the independent Maize 282 association panel; neutral demographic models place fewer than 2% of simulated windows in its 5% tails. The lower tail, the sweep like windows, holds as many bubbles as the rest but simpler ones, mostly large TE presence-absence variants; the upper tail, with an excess of intermediate frequency alleles, holds the most complex ones. This holds across window sizes and recombination rates and within the temperate lines, and the graph's structural variant allele frequencies agree. The structural context of a gene shows in its expression: genes confined to complex bubbles are expressed in fewer tissues than genes in conserved intervals, and 1,707 genes differ in expression between NAM founders with different structural variant alleles. Structural complexity in maize is thus TE generated standing variation, reduced by hard sweeps and preserved by maintained polymorphism, not a target of selection, and reflected in gene expression.

papers.title: Comparative Metagenomic Analysis of Chondrosia and Chondrilla Sponge Microbiomes Reveals Distinct Symbiotic Communities, Functional Potential, and Contrasting Environmental Responses
papers.abstract: Marine sponges frequently maintain distinct, host-specific microbial communities despite inhabiting overlapping or identical environments. In this study, we performed comparative shotgun metagenomic sequencing on two sympatric sponge taxa, Chondrilla and Chondrosia, collected from the same shallow-water habitat in the Florida Keys to examine whether differences in microbiome composition and functional potential persist under shared environmental conditions. Morphological examination and phylogenetic analyses of nuclear 18S rRNA sequences confirmed the taxonomic placement of the green specimens within Chondrilla and the black specimens within Chondrosia sp. Community-level profiling revealed taxonomic differences between the two hosts: the Chondrilla microbiome exhibited a strong enrichment of Cyanobacteriota, notably Candidatus Synechococcus spongiarum, whereas the Chondrosia microbiome was characterized by Poribacteria, Chloroflexota, Nitrosopumilales, and other sponge-associated lineages. Functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) identified distinct functional potential between the two microbiomes, particularly regarding pathways associated with osmoregulation, oxidative and environmental stress responses, and secondary-metabolite biosynthesis, including diverse biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) such as terpenes and RiPPs. Additionally, parallel physiological monitoring during a freshwater exposure experiment demonstrated contrasting environmental responses, with Chondrosia exhibiting long-term survival over ten months under static low-salinity conditions compared to rapid deterioration in Chondrilla. Together, our findings provide genome-resolved evidence that sympatric sponge hosts maintain distinct microbial assemblages and functional profiles, establishing a framework for future investigations linking sponge-microbe interactions, biosynthetic potential, and stress resilience.

papers.title: A stratified benchmark reveals distinct short- and long-read performance gradients within difficult genomic regions
papers.abstract: Accurate detection of small variants underpins population, functional and clinical genomics, yet short-read sequencing remains unreliable in repetitive and duplicated regions of the human genome, where long reads provide substantially greater sequence context. Although this disparity is well documented, aggregate accuracy metrics delineate where short- and long-read callsets diverge but not the mechanisms that give rise to these differences. Here, we present a region-stratified benchmark of single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) and insertion--deletion (INDEL) detection from Illumina short-read and PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing of the Genome in a Bottle reference sample HG002, evaluating multiple variant callers across genomic contexts, sequencing depths and INDEL lengths. Both platforms achieved near-complete accuracy in high-confidence regions, whereas short-read performance deteriorated in low-mappability regions and segmental duplications, a deficit that persisted with increasing sequencing depth. Within these regions, short-read recall declined toward the interiors of long tracts, with increasing sequence identity to the closest paralog and with greater distance from paralogous sequence variants, and these declines coincided with a pronounced excess of ambiguously placed reads. Together, these findings implicate ambiguous read placement as the predominant source of the short-read deficit, demonstrate that its magnitude can be anticipated from the length and paralog similarity of the surrounding sequence, and thereby delineate the genomic contexts in which long-read sequencing is most warranted.

papers.title: The genome sequence of the reef-building coral Cyphastrea microphthalma from the Persian/Arabian Gulf
papers.abstract: We present a genome assembly from the coral species Cyphastrea microphthalma from the southern Persian/Arabian Gulf (Cnidaria; Anthozoa; Hexacorallia; Scleractinia; Merulinidae). The assembly is 681.2 Mb in size, spanning 5,554 scaffolds with a contig N50 of 244.4 kb. The assembly has a BUSCO completeness of 94.1% (single = 85.1%, duplicated = 9%, fragmented = 1.6%, missing = 4.3%) using the metazoa_odb10 reference set (n = 954). Genome annotation identified 24,716 protein-coding genes (including 10 pseudogenes) and a high repeat content of 63.4%. The mitochondrial genome has also been assembled and is 17.9 kb in length.

papers.title: Genotoxic stress and clonal expansion shape the somatic genome of systemic sclerosis skin
papers.abstract: Background: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a life-limiting inflammatory disease characterised by skin and visceral fibrosis. We previously showed that fibrotic skin from patients with diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) accumulates a large number of somatic mutations, although the mechanisms that generate them and their disease-related consequences remain poorly understood. We investigated the burden, clonal architecture and biological significance of somatic mutations in dermal sections from patients with dcSSc ( 25 %) had a sequence linked with oxidative guanine damage (C>A), pointing to ongoing DNA damage and cellular stress. The C>A burden was higher in dcSSc than in lcSSc and correlated with the modified Rodnan skin score - a clinical measurement of skin fibrosis severity. Variant burden increased with patient age but not with disease duration. AHSCT did not change the mutational landscape. Conclusions: Fibrosis skin in SSc is characterized by a widespread somatic mosaicism generated by ongoing mutagenesis attributable to oxidative DNA damage. Persistence of mutant clones after regression of fibrosis argues against their being sufficient drivers of the fibrotic phenotype and identifies the somatic genome as a record of cellular injury.

papers.title: AHCY inhibition reshapes DNA methylation and transcriptional regulation in colorectal cancer cells
papers.abstract: DNA methylation is an important epigenetic mechanism regulating gene expression, and its maintenance depends on cellular methyl group metabolism. Adenosylhomocysteinase (AHCY) is a key enzyme in the methionine cycle that hydrolyzes S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), thereby preventing its accumulation and inhibition of methyltransferase activity. Although AHCY has been implicated in cancer cell proliferation and transcriptional regulation, the effects of its inhibition on genome-wide DNA methylation and their relationship to gene expression remain poorly understood in colorectal cancer (CRC). Here, we investigated the consequences of pharmacological AHCY inhibition in GP5d colorectal cancer cells by integrating metabolomic profiling, nanopore sequencing-based DNA methylation analysis and RNA sequencing. AHCY inhibition resulted in SAH accumulation, widespread DNA hypomethylation and reduced cell proliferation, accompanied by changes in purine metabolism and gene expression. Despite the overall loss of DNA methylation, localized hypermethylation was also observed, particularly at CpG-rich regulatory regions. Transcriptomic analysis revealed changes in proliferation-associated and cell cycle checkpoint pathways, including strong upregulation of the cell cycle regulator CDKN1A. Importantly, promoter hypomethylation was significantly enriched among upregulated genes, including genes involved in cell cycle regulation, whereas gene body hypomethylation showed no comparable association with differential gene expression. Together, these findings demonstrate that AHCY inhibition induces extensive metabolic, epigenetic and transcriptional changes in CRC cells and suggest that promoter hypomethylation may contribute to the transcriptional responses associated with reduced cell proliferation.

papers.title: A Framework for Identifying Determinants of Epigenomic State: Decoding Variable CTCF Occupancy and Contact Frequency
papers.abstract: CTCF binding is essential for delineating topologically associated domains, constraining enhancer-promoter interactions, and controlling gene expression. Many CTCF peaks are bound in all cell-types, but the mechanisms regulating cell-type-specific CTCF occupancy are not fully understood. Here, we present a general framework to comprehensively discover factors driving variable epigenomic state and TF occupancy. We apply this framework to CTCF ChIP-seq binding across hundreds of cell/tissues, and we identify five distinct mechanisms regulating CTCF occupancy. In addition to known mechanisms of DNA methylation and cell-type-specific TF co-binding, we find that the largest set of variable-occupancy sites is modulated by CTCF expression levels. Variable peaks have weaker-affinity, and their occupancy is modulated by either higher CTCF levels or flanking TFs. We evaluate the predictive power on CTCF occupancy in held-out samples. Finally, we show that variable CTCF binding predicts differential contact frequency, chromatin loop structure, and upregulation of gene expression.

papers.title: Genomic conformation reflects epigenetic programming rather than gene expression
papers.abstract: Genome function is regulated temporally and tissue-specifically through coordinated interplay between epigenetic modifications and genomic elements, however, the extent to which chromatin conformation shapes or is shaped by epigenetic programming and transcriptional activity in vivo, remains largely unresolved. Through analysis of the well-characterised Dlk1-Dio3 imprinted domain, we have identified tissue and parent-of-origin specific conformations and taken a genetic approach to determine the hierarchical relationships between conformation, epigenetic state and transcription. Parental-origin specific topological domains identified in fetal brain are dependent on the germline-derived imprinting control region. In the absence of specific CTCF binding at a secondary imprinting control element, the parental origin-specific CTCF-mediated conformation can be disrupted without a change to domain-wide imprinting, transcription or epigenetic state. These findings indicate that, in this developmental context, conformation can be decoupled from transcription and that each can be independently governed by a hierarchy of epigenetically controlled regulatory features initiated in the germline.

papers.title: A Comparative Metagenomic Analysis of the Viral Diversity in Faecal Samples from Malnourished and Non-malnourished Children with Gastroenteritis Admitted at Victoria Mxenge Hospital in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
papers.abstract: Viral gastroenteritis and malnutrition remain major health burdens among children under five in South Africa. Malnourished children are particularly vulnerable to prolonged enteric viral infections, yet their gut virome remains poorly characterised in South Africa. This study compared gut virome diversity among malnourished and non-malnourished children with gastroenteritis, and children without gastroenteritis and malnutrition (healthy controls). This retrospective laboratory-based continuation study analysed 69 faecal samples from age-matched children aged 0- 36 months at Victoria Mxenge Hospital across three cohorts: malnourished children with gastroenteritis, non-malnourished children with gastroenteritis, and healthy controls. Viral metagenomic sequencing was performed using Illumina NextSeq 2000, followed by bioinformatic analyses. Virome profiling identified 39 viral families, 71 genera, and 243 species. Of the total sequenced reads, 60.4% were classified comprising 91.0% mapped to bacteria, 6.4% to viruses, and 2.6% to human host and other microorganisms. Eukaryotic viral reads were highest among non-malnourished children with gastroenteritis (37.2%), followed by healthy controls (32.3%) and malnourished children with gastroenteritis (30.5%). Detected enteric viral families included, Sedoreoviridae, Caliciviridae, Picornaviridae, Astroviridae, and Adenoviridae, with Sedoreoviridae being predominant. Multiple co-detections of enteric viruses were observed. Significant cohorts differences occurred in viral diversity (p = 0.0038) and abundance (p = 0.0001), but not in evenness (p = 0.146) and richness (p = 0.0896). This study revealed differences in faecal virome composition across cohorts and provides baseline genomic data for viral surveillance. The findings highlight the importance of vaccination, nutritional and preventive strategies to curb infant mortality associated with gastroenteritis and malnutrition in South Africa.

papers.title: Genomic insertion sequence populations of an ancient chemosynthetic symbiont
papers.abstract: Genetic isolation as a consequence of host restriction of bacterial symbionts can lead to reductive genome evolution resulting in small, functionally streamlined genomes that are biased toward high AT contents. Frequently, reductive genome evolution leads to the loss of transposable elements, which are one of the major initial drivers of symbiont genome evolution through massive expansion events following initial host restriction. Under specific circumstances, where host-restricted bacteria continue to experience genetic mixing, transposable elements are retained in and, in some cases, introduced to symbiont genomes, even in ancient symbioses. Very little is known about these transposable element populations, regarding density, diversity, and activity as well as their influence on symbiont evolution and physiology. Here, we explored genomic population dynamics of insertion sequence (IS) elements, a type of transposable element, in 647 genomes of the chemosynthetic Gammaproteobacteria symbiont Candidatus Thiosymbion from three distantly related marine invertebrate hosts. We observed host-group specific patterns of genomic properties, likely reflective of symbiont genome evolution driven by varying degrees of genetic isolation due to differences in symbiont localization (ecto- to endosymbiont). We found that Thiosymbion genomes had highly diverse and dynamic IS populations, which varied by both symbiont localization and symbiont lineage with instances of clade-specific gain, loss, and expansion of certain IS families. Combined, our results suggest that variable IS expansion in Thiosymbion likely contributes to high intraspecific variability in genome structure.

papers.title: A sequence context-unbiased approach to enable precise inference of mutational processes in cancer.
papers.abstract: Mutational signatures are recurring patterns of somatic mutations observed in cancer genomes, resulting from the activity of endogenous and exogenous mutagenic processes. Their investigation has significantly advanced our understanding of cancer etiology, informing prevention strategies and supporting clinical stratification. Although analytical approaches facilitate the identification of mutational signatures, their biological interpretation can be challenging, as some signatures may reflect methodological artifacts rather than distinct underlying mutational processes. Conventional mutational signatures inference frameworks generally assume that mutational opportunities are uniformly distributed across the genome and comparable across cancer types. However, mutable DNA motifs are not evenly distributed throughout the genome and their accessibility to DNA repair machinery is influenced by local chromatin states. To address these limitations, we developed SEQUENCE (SEQuence context Ubiased InferENCE of mutational signaturEs), a method that accounts for the heterogeneous nucleotide composition by generating weighted mutation catalogues, in which each mutation is adjusted for the local availability of its respective sequence context. By using SEQUENCE-generated mutation matrices as input for SigProfilerExtractor, a conventional framework for mutational signature extraction, we demonstrate that our approach mitigates biases arising from cell-type specific and locally varying mutational rates across the genome. Furthermore, the latent local information encoded in the weights enables the disentanglement of co-occurring mutational processes targeting the same sequence context and refines the mutational spectra of previously described mutational signatures. Mutational signatures characterised by relatively flat mutational spectra are notoriously difficult to extract. Here, using clinically relevant mutational signatures, we demonstrate that SEQUENCE can improve patient stratification according to their response to adjuvant chemotherapy. Together, these findings highlight sequence context unbiased mutational signature inference as a promising new framework for revisiting current reference signatures, providing deeper insight into their underlying origins and facilitating their translation into cancer prevention and clinical application.

papers.title: Epstein-Barr Virus Load in Lymphoblastoid Cell Lines and Its Association with Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Background: Blood Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNAs are reported to have genetic determinants and correlate with prevalence of autoimmune, neurological, respiratory and cardiovascular condition. However, whether a patient is more susceptible to EBV virus infection is unknown. Lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) are often immortalized by infecting individuals' peripheral lymphocytes by EBV in a dish, providing an ex vivo model to address this question. Here, we examined associations of EBV viral load in LCLs with schizophrenia (SCZ) diagnosis, SCZ and bipolar (BIP) polygenic risk scores, and host genetic variation. Methods: EBV viral load in LCLs from the Molecular Genetics of Schizophrenia (MGS) study was examined using univariable and multivariable linear regression. Separate multivariable models evaluated SCZ diagnosis, bipolar disorder polygenic score (BIP-PGS), and SCZ polygenic score (SCZ-PGS), adjusting for age, sex, and the first five genetic ancestry principal components. An exploratory analysis examined age at schizophrenia onset. A genome-wide association study (GWAS) was conducted in 2,000 participants using the same covariates. Results: SCZ diagnosis was not significantly associated with EBV viral load after covariate adjustment (Beta=-0.004, SE = 0.025, P = 0.868). Neither BIP-PGS (Beta=-0.009, SE = 0.013, P = 0.469) nor SCZ-PGS (Beta=-0.002, SE = 0.013, P = 0.897) was significantly associated with viral load. Univariable analyses also identified no significant association with age at SCZ onset. For GWAS of EBV loads in LCL, no variant reached genome-wide significance (P < 5 x 10e-8). The strongest association was observed at rs7188098 in the GP2 gene on chromosome 16 (P = 3.7 x 10e-7). Conclusions: These analyses did not identify statistically significant associations of LCL EBV viral load with SCZ diagnosis or the psychiatric polygenic scores examined. The GWAS identified suggestive signals of association with EBV load, which require further investigation in larger sample sizes.

papers.title: Benchmarking sequence-to-function models and mapping enhancer-gene interactions with E2GScore
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function models predict gene expression and chromatin features directly from DNA sequence and are increasingly used to infer enhancer-gene regulatory interactions. However, differences in attribution procedures and benchmarking datasets complicate comparisons between models, while the biological information captured by their enhancer-gene scores remains poorly understood. Here we introduce E2GScore, a unified framework for extracting and benchmarking enhancer-gene predictions from sequence-to-function models. By systematically varying scoring protocols, we identify gene-readout normalization and cell-type-matched expression tracks as important determinants of performance, whereas in silico mutagenesis offers no advantage over less computationally demanding input gradients. We compare seven sequence-to-function models and three established enhancer-gene predictors against CRISPR interference screens in K562 cells and primary human astrocytes. AlphaGenome 1 and 2 outperformed all other sequence-to-function models, and matched or outperformed experimentally informed predictors, particularly for distal enhancers, without a statistically significant difference between AlphaGenome versions after multiple-testing correction. We further show that the apparent reduction in predictive performance in astrocytes relative to K562 cells observed across models results primarily from differences in benchmarking dataset composition, particularly enhancer-TSS distance and target-gene expression. Using the open-weight AlphaGenome 1, we then generated E2GMap, a genome-wide resource of enhancer-gene regulation comprising 14.7 billion enhancer-gene attribution scores across 454 human biosamples, 45% of which are absent from existing enhancer-gene maps such as those from ENCODE-rE2G and AlphaGenome 2. E2GMap is available at e2gscore.com. Together, E2GScore and E2GMap establish a framework for rigorous evaluation of sequence-based enhancer-gene predictions and provide an extensible resource for studying gene regulation across human cell types and tissues.

papers.title: ONTOLOGY™: Streamlined DNA Barcoding and Metabarcoding on Nanopore
papers.abstract: Nanopore sequencers have unlocked the potential for a distributed network of DNA barcoding and metabarcoding laboratories. However, the realization of this potential confronts two challenges--one molecular, one computational. First, rigorous indexing protocols are critical to correctly associate sequences with their source specimen or sample; and second, data interpretation often demands processing millions of indexed reads in a structured fashion via complex bioinformatic pipelines. ONTOLOGY addresses these challenges. At its core lies a graphical user interface (GUI) that guides users through the workflow from specimen or sample reception to the generation of DNA barcode records or metabarcode files. To facilitate data acquisition, it includes freeze-dried PCR plates that uniquely tag the amplicons from each well, hence supporting sample-sequence association. The ONTOLOGY GUI is constructed around two core workflows that process data from a sequencing Run. The Barcode Inference Pipeline (BIP) delineates the OTU(s) recovered from each well and designates them as target or non-target sequences via comparison of OTU sequences to a reference sequence library. The Metabarcoding Analysis Pipeline (MAP) processes sequence arrays derived from bulk samples (organismal or environmental DNA) and infers the species represented while rigorously excluding false positives. To validate ONTOLOGY, we present an original data analysis completed via both pipelines. Built for maximum flexibility, ONTOLOGY also supports the analysis of custom experiments. By employing a GUI to coordinate passage through the workflows with structured amplicon tagging and informatics pipelines, ONTOLOGY facilitates the molecular analyses needed to advance biodiversity science via decentralization. Plates and software can be obtained from www.ontology.bio.

papers.title: RepeatViewer: a platform for explorative analysis of repetitive DNAs
papers.abstract: RepeatViewer is a graphical user interface application designed for repetitive sequence inspection and curation, especially focusing on, but not limited to, transposable elements (TEs). It automatically identifies structural features of TEs, including long terminal repeats (LTRs), terminal inverted repeats (TIRs), and target side duplications (TSDs). All detected and user-defined annotations can be interactively inspected, edited, and exported. RepeatViewer also integrates a TE curation workflow intended to facilitate their manual refinement. In addition, it provides interactive visualization of TE sequences and genome-wide TE annotations, such as dot plots as well as TE distribution and divergence analyses. RepeatViewer is modularly built and can be easily customized by the user.

papers.title: Publicly Available Genomic Evidence for Nipah and Avian Influenza Viruses in Bangladesh: A Scoping Assessment of Metadata Completeness and Surveillance Representativeness at the Human-Animal Interface
papers.abstract: Bangladesh experiences recurrent Nipah virus (NiV) outbreaks and sustained avian influenza virus (AIV) activity. Whether public genomic records contain metadata needed to assess surveillance representativeness across hosts, locations, and time is unclear.We conducted a structured, source-based scoping assessment of publicly documented NiV and AIV genomic records from Bangladesh (2001-2025), drawing on NCBI GenBank/INSDC and cited peer-reviewed and public-health sources. A pilot registry contained 108 entries (55 NiV, 53 AIV). Metadata were retained only when explicitly reported; unverified fields were recorded as not extracted. The registry is not a complete census. Five analytical questions were prespecified; several could not be evaluated because accession-level metadata were unavailable. The 33-accession AIV set containing H5N1 and H3N8 was excluded from H5/H9-specific interpretation. In the pilot registry, 9/108 entries (8.3%) had explicitly reported host species; the separate host-implied category was not added. Twelve entries (11.1%) had a full collection date; 21 (19.4%) had any collection date. Eight entries (7.4%) had an explicit district. The registry lists 22 NiV accession identifiers from a 2026 study, whereas the publication reports 23 newly sequenced N-gene records; this remains unresolved. Eight AIV accessions (PV961349.1-PV961356.1) represent eight segments of one chicken H5N1 isolate, not eight genomes. Twelve MN994-series records are HA-gene sequences from environmental live-bird-market samples.The pilot registry demonstrates substantial metadata limitations. Explicit host information was available for 8.3% of entries and explicit district for 7.4%; these prevent reliable quantitative assessment of host, district-level, and temporal representativeness and do not establish absence of surveillance or viral circulation. Accession-level reconstruction with transparent verification tiers and harmonised identifiers is required before quantitative representativeness indices or district-level priorities can be calculated.

papers.title: Chromosome-scale genome assembly of multinucleate heterokaryotic Rhizoctonia solani AG1-IB
papers.abstract: Rhizoctonia solani AG1-IB is an economically important fungal pathogen of turfgrass and agricultural crops, yet available genome assemblies remain fragmented or represent collapsed or consensus sequences that obscure haplotype-specific variation, limiting investigations of genome evolution and heterokaryosis. Here, we present a chromosome-scale, haplotype-aware genome assembly of AG1-IB isolate S1W6 generated using Oxford Nanopore sequencing, Hi-C scaffolding, and short-read polishing. De novo assembly with PECAT produced two haplotype-aware nuclear genome assemblies, with BUSCO completeness greater than 96% and nuclear genome N50 values exceeding 2 Mb. Comparative analyses revealed substantial haplotype divergence, with over 600,000 SNPs and 80,000 indels between haplotypes with 97.75% average nucleotide identity separating assemblies. FastANI analyses showed comparable genetic divergence between Hap1 and Hap2 assemblies of S1W6 to that observed among independently collected AG1-IB isolates from different plant hosts and geographic regions. Despite extensive nucleotide variation, Gene Ontology profiles, predicted effector repertoires, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and biosynthetic gene cluster composition were conserved between assemblies. In contrast, homeodomain (HD) mating-type loci were variable. Hap2 contained four HD genes (W-HD1, W-HD2, E-HD1, and E-HD2), whereas Hap1 lacked E-HD1, and shared divergent HD amino acid sequences. A STE3 pheromone receptor gene on chromosome 15 was highly conserved in both haplotypes. This study provides the first chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome resource for R. solani AG1-IB and demonstrates that heterokaryotic individuals can harbor genomic variation approaching the levels observed among genetically diverse isolates of AG1-IB. These findings highlight the importance of haplotype-aware assemblies for understanding genome evolution and mating-type diversity in heterokaryotic fungal plant pathogens.

papers.title: scOnion: Cross-Modal Concordance-Aware Joint Analysis of Cells and Features in Single-Cell Multiomic Data
papers.abstract: Single-cell multiomic assays jointly profile gene expression and chromatin accessibility in the same cells, enabling direct analysis of cross-layer coordination. However, agreement between modalities varies across cells, and existing integration methods often emphasize shared structure, potentially averaging away cell-specific cross-modal discordance that carries biological signal. Here we present scOnion, a concordance-aware computational framework that quantifies cross-modality agreement and propagates this information into downstream analyses. Starting from paired low-rank representations obtained by spectral integration, scOnion computes per-cell concordance scores, a concordance-aware joint cell embedding, and an induced cross-modal feature embedding. The cell embedding preserves structure strongly represented in either modality, improving cell-type and state resolution, while the feature embedding scores candidate regulatory element(rE)-to-gene (rE2G) pairs. Across immune, neural, and developmental functional genomic datasets, scOnion's concordance patterns are reproducible and cell-resolved, with low-concordance cells enriched for modality-specific structure. scOnion also prioritizes candidate rE2G pairs, including distal links, with stronger support from external Hi-C contacts and fine-mapped eQTL data than the baseline linkage methods. In a B-cell fate bifurcation study, scOnion reveals remodeling of concordance and rE2G coupling during lineage commitment. scOnion embeds ~70,000 cells and computes rE2G links on CPU in 30 minutes, extends naturally to other multiomic assays such as CITE-seq, and is available as open-source software.

papers.title: Heterogeneous Effects Across Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) Driver Mutations Challenges a Unified Model of CHIP
papers.abstract: Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is an age-associated expansion of hematopoietic stem cells harboring somatic mutations in the absence of overt malignancy. CHIP driver genes impart divergent effects on many biological processes, yet the mechanisms underlying these gene-specific effects, particularly in non-hematologic disease contexts, remain poorly understood. We analyzed 466 samples from the Multi-Ancestry Genomics, Epigenomics, and Transcriptomics of Alzheimer's Disease dataset, and identified function-specific differences between CHIP categorizations. Uniquely, DNMT3A CHIP was associated with global hypomethylation, STAG2 CHIP increased mutation burden, HSC differentiation CHIP strongly triggered adaptive immune response, and proliferative signaling CHIP induced coagulation and cell adhesion. These divergent functions differentially modulate inflammatory pathways and suggest investigating CHIP's downstream effects through a driver gene function-based approach rather than treating CHIP as a single entity. Our multi-omics analyses provide such a framework to improve mechanistic interpretation of conflicting relationships between CHIP and diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

papers.title: Structural and functional reference maps of transcriptional enhancers in the developing human cortex
papers.abstract: Non-coding regulatory variation is the major driver of human phenotypic diversity, yet maps of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their variability across developmental cell types remain limited. Here, we integrated single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from 54 mid-gestation human prenatal cortical donors to generate a CRE atlas comprising 1,165,697 candidate CREs across 104,266 cortical nuclei. Chromatin-state annotation classified 1.5% of CREs as bivalent promoters, 0.3% as active promoters, 39.8% as active distal enhancers, 1.3% as CTCF-associated insulators but 57.1% remain unresolved. Overlap with an external enhancer assay dataset showed that many unresolved CREs, nevertheless, exhibit regulatory activity; thus, current chromatin signatures underestimate the functional regulatory landscape. Pseudo-bulk analysis across major cortical lineages revealed that the prenatal cortical regulome is dominated by lineage-restricted CREs, with only a small core shared across all lineages. Restricted CREs were enriched for unresolved elements, intermediate-sharing classes were enhancer-dominant, and broadly shared CREs showed the strongest promoter-proximal and bivalent contribution. Lineage-selective transcription factor (TF) sequence grammar analyses identified progenitor-associated homeodomain programs and neuronal basic helix-loop-helix signatures, together with representative candidate regulators such as SOX10, NFIA, EMX2, DLX1, ARX, and RFX3. Across donors, developmental time, and sex, prenatal cortical CREs segregated into a stable versus variable regulatory compartments. Broadly, recurrent and developmentally persistent CREs had greater activity, on average, and greater enrichment for promoter-associated states, whereas donor-restricted and temporally restricted CREs had lower activity and were enriched for unresolved and enhancer-like elements. Sex-biased CREs were rare but highly specific: female-biased CREs were predominantly X-linked, broadly shared, and developmentally persistent, whereas male-biased CREs were more numerous, less resolved, and more restricted across lineage and developmental contexts. Together, these results define the prenatal cortical regulatory landscape at single-cell resolution, revealing a small, stable, promoter-rich core and a larger variable, enhancer- and unresolved-rich compartment in which lineage diversification is driven primarily by selective deployment of distal regulatory elements.

papers.title: Differential gene expression profiling of lumbar disc degeneration in the RuDDS cohort
papers.abstract: Lumbar disc degeneration disease (LDDD) is a major structural cause of low back pain, one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, and has no disease-modifying treatment. We performed RNA sequencing of 72 intraoperative intervertebral disc samples from the Russian disc degeneration study (RuDDS) cohort, comparing severe (Pfirrmann grades IV-V) with moderate (grade III) degeneration. We identified 731 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 347 upregulated and 384 downregulated in severely degenerated discs) in the 57 samples that passed quality control. Upregulated DEGs were enriched for extracellular matrix organisation, ossification, and TGF-beta; and Hippo signalling, whereas downregulated DEGs were enriched for immune and inflammatory processes. We identified five differentially active transcription factors, including the TGF-beta; effectors SMAD3 and SMAD4 and the osteogenic regulator DLX5. Of the five, only DLX5 was also a DEG. DEGs were enriched for LDDD-associated genes from Open Targets (odds ratio = 1.68, P = 3.37 * 10-6). Connectivity mapping against the LINCS L1000 database showed that histone deacetylase inhibitors and glucocorticoids reverse the signature of severe degeneration. Together, these results point to TGF-beta-driven fibrotic and osteogenic remodelling as the dominant transcriptional feature of severe disc degeneration, and prioritise candidate genes and compounds for functional validation.

papers.title: Functional interrogation of osteoarthritis-associated regulatory variants and effector genes.
papers.abstract: Background: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with osteoarthritis (OA); however, the regulatory variants and effector genes underlying most associations remain unresolved. Results: We used complementary functional genomic approaches in chondrocytes to resolve prioritized OA risk loci. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) in primary human chondrocytes identified allele-specific regulatory activity at variants across multiple loci, two of which were independently validated using low-throughput reporter assays. In parallel, integration of OA GWAS signals with chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac CUT&Tag, and chromatin conformation data prioritised candidate regulatory elements for CRISPR based perturbation. CRISPR activation and interference supported functional regulatory relationships between OA risk regions and Pappalysin 1 (PAPPA) and Sprouty RTK signaling antagonist 4 (SPRY4) as target genes. At the 9q33 locus, multiple independent lines of evidence converged on rs1895062, which resides in an accessible region that loops to the PAPPA promoter. The OA risk G allele at rs1895062 results in higher regulatory activity by MPRA and low throughput reporter assay. Activation of this region by CRISPR increases PAPPA gene expression and induces widespread transcriptional changes involving extracellular matrix remodelling and other OA-relevant pathways. Conclusion: Integrating genetic association, genomic and epigenomic data, and functional perturbation in disease-relevant cells can resolve the regulatory mechanisms underlying OA risk loci. Using this multi-faceted approach, we provide convergent functional evidence for rs1895062 as a likely causal variant that controls PAPPA gene expression and OA risk.

papers.title: Clonal landscape of human nephrons
papers.abstract: The nephron is a highly compartmentalized structure, where distinct patterns of somatic mosaicism may be established and contribute to altered kidney functions with aging. Here we show extensive remodeling of aged nephrons by mosaic clones using integrated sequencing of >1,000 microdissected samples collected from anatomically distinct nephron segments. Striking differences were observed across segments. Proximal tubules exhibited markedly higher mutation burdens with mutational signatures characteristic of clear cell renal cell carcinoma and larger clonal expansion than other segments. Cancer-related mutations were observed only infrequently and largely limited to proximal tubules, while copy number abnormalities were quite common, most frequently involving chromosomes 18, 10, 7, X, 22, 3 and 9, in a segment-specific manner. Clone size appears to depend more on cell turnover than on driver events. Particularly, in collecting ducts, numerous clones independently acquiring chromosome 18 loss evolved over years and ultimately replaced 15-47% of collecting duct cells in aged donors despite minimal increase in their clone size, likely reflecting strong fitness advantage of chromosome 18-deficient clones under slow tissue turnover. Chromosome 18-deficient cells significantly correlated with fibrosis and showed reduced expression of chromosome 18 genes, including those involved in sodium handling (NEDD4L) and TGF-{beta} signaling (SMAD2/4/7). In line with this, GSEA of chromosome 18-deficient cells revealed enhanced hallmark pathways overlapping those associated with acute kidney injury that are related to TGF-{beta} signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and inflammatory responses. These findings illustrate how nephrons are remodeled with aging, providing insights into the role of somatic remodelling in altered kidney structures and functions with aging.

papers.title: Alternative splicing edits intrinsically disordered regions across human protein isoforms
papers.abstract: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) lack a stable three-dimensional structure, yet they mediate many of the interactions and regulatory functions of proteins. Alternative splicing produces multiple protein isoforms from a single gene, and because individual exons can encode all or part of an IDR, splicing has the potential to add, remove or reshape disordered regions. However, it remains unclear whether splicing preferentially acts on disordered sequence in all kinds of proteins, how it changes an IDR from one isoform to another, and how this relationship arose during evolution. Here, we map predicted disorder onto the coding exons and genomic codons of human protein isoforms, which allows any two isoforms of a gene to be compared directly, and analyze this map across protein classes and families. We find that alternatively spliced exons are more disordered than constitutive exons in every class of protein, from transcription factors to metabolic enzymes, and that splicing usually changes IDRs at their ends, adding or removing disordered segments as modular units rather than cutting through them. The disordered sequence that splicing varies is compositionally distinct from the disorder that all isoforms share. Notably, the apparent loss of disorder over gene evolution reflects differences between protein families rather than change within them, whereas exons whose splice sites are conserved in few mammals encode more disorder than the other exons of the same gene, with a composition resembling that of young genes. Our results suggest that alternative splicing treats intrinsic disorder as a modular, evolvable layer of protein architecture, and that exons with poorly conserved splice sites may be one route by which disordered sequence enters proteins.

papers.title: No evidence of genome-wide selection against sensetranscription starts in human introns
papers.abstract: RNA polymerase II often starts transcription inside genes, usually at elements that initiate in both directions. An intragenic start pointing in the gene's direction (a sense start) makes RNA that passes the gene's splice sites and polyadenylation signals and may interfere with the gene. Introns may therefore have lost sequences that start sense transcription. In PRO-cap data from K562 and HCT116 cells, the sense start at intronic elements, measured against the antisense start, is a fifth to a third weaker than at intergenic elements of similar read depth. Sequence models that have never seen an element's chromosome predict 30-42% of this bias from local DNA, except models trained on K562 applied to HCT116. However, introns as a whole show little or no depletion of predicted sense starts, and among 76,215 human genomes, variants predicted to create sense starts are not kept rarer than those creating antisense starts. In both cell lines, and in K562 GRO-cap data, strong measured start sites are rarer on the gene strand, mainly near the 5'' end of active genes. Thus, weaker sense starts appear to be a feature of individual active elements, partly predictable from their sequence, and we find no sign that selection has removed such sequences from introns.

papers.title: Transcription starting inside human introns is widespread but mostly yields short-lived RNA
papers.abstract: Background: Thousands of annotated long non-coding RNAs lie inside introns of protein-coding genes, on the host's strand, but whether they are independent genes or pieces of host transcripts is usually unknown. An independent gene needs its own start site. Results: We mapped transcription starts inside introns, using nascent capped RNA from two human cell lines. The approach detected the start sites of 94% of clearly expressed protein-coding genes nested in introns and confirmed 1,346 and 3,061 intronic start sites, almost all unannotated. Most are cell-type-specific, carrying active chromatin marks and motifs of the cell's key transcription factors. Many initiate as strongly as the hosts' alternative promoters but rarely sustain transcription: after a synchronised restart of transcription, their nascent RNA fades within a few kilobases, their short transcripts are partly degraded by the nuclear exosome, and the sequence downstream rarely has the early splice-donor site that protects promoter transcripts. Per initiation event, they leave about as little stable RNA as start sites between genes, so host transcription does not explain their low output. Expressed intronic RNAs on the host's strand more often lack their own start site than those on the opposite strand. Conclusions: Transcription starting inside human introns is widespread but mostly yields short-lived RNA. Many intronic long non-coding RNAs on the host's strand are therefore likely to be pieces of host transcripts rather than independent genes, which matters for their annotation. All intronic start sites in both cell lines, with every measure used here, are provided as a resource.

papers.title: Population genomics of the Anopheles farauti complex reveals a distinct regime of malaria vector evolution in the southwest Pacific
papers.abstract: Abstract: The southwest Pacific has one of the highest per-capita malaria burdens outside Africa, yet how its malaria mosquitoes evolve is largely unknown. In African vectors, insecticide resistance evolves rapidly in large, connected populations carrying abundant standing variation. Southwest Pacific vectors show little to no biochemical resistance despite decades of insecticide-based control. We analyse 495 genomes from six taxa of the Anopheles farauti complex, which includes the region's major vectors. The complex radiated rapidly in the late Pleistocene concomitant to the peopling of Near Oceania. Thereafter, post-glacial sea-level rise and climate change fragmented its populations into recently colonised island isolates. Successive environmental and colonisation bottlenecks left a legacy of extraordinary inbreeding, most marked in island populations of the coastal specialist An. farauti sensu stricto, where sustained low effective population size has allowed deleterious alleles to be purged effectively; the inland generalists An. hinesorum and An. oreios retain more variation. After five decades of chemical control we recover a single resistance sweep, at Gste2, alongside recent selection at species-specific chemosensory gene repertoires. Severe inbreeding and the loss of standing variation have not prevented ecological success, challenging assumptions about how much variation and connectivity a vector population needs to thrive. This work establishes the first genomic foundation for this major vector system of endemic species through a biogeographically diverse region of the world.
